172: Karyotype 46,XX: one of the two X chromosomes is randomly inactivated in each cell (lyonisation). The long non-coding RNA XIST (pink dots) coats the chromosome in cis and recruits PRC2 (H3K27me3): compact chromatin pressed against the envelope.
174: The largest condensate in the nucleus: no membrane, but three nested, immiscible liquid phases. It forms around the nucleolar organisers, the ribosomal DNA repeats on the short arms of chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21 and 22 (about 400 copies per diploid genome, a number that varies widely between individuals; roughly half are active). Its surface is lined with heterochromatin (NAD domains, ≈ 4 % of the genome). It dissolves at mitosis and re-forms in telophase. Shrink to 30 nm or less and come close: you can enter it.
175: Irregularly shaped condensate (20 to 50 per nucleus) made of 20–25 nm interchromatin granules. At the core (pink): the proteins SON and SRRM2, without which it dissolves. Around them: SR proteins (cyan) and snRNPs (blue). At the periphery: the long non-coding RNA MALAT1 (orange). No DNA and no transcription inside: it is a reserve of splicing factors in constant exchange with the nucleoplasm. Genes sitting against it are spliced more efficiently — as is HBB right next to it.
177: A 0.1 to 2 µm sphere described in 1903 by Santiago Ramón y Cajal in neurons (the “accessory body” of the nucleolus). Scaffold: coilin (orange). A workshop for small RNPs: chemical retouching of snRNAs by scaRNPs (green); assembly of U4/U6 then of the U4/U6·U5 tri-snRNP and recycling after each splicing event (blue); snoRNP maturation; telomerase assembly in cells that express it. Numerous in neurons and rapidly proliferating cells, rare or absent in many resting adult cells; it re-forms when transcription resumes.
179: A spherical shell of PML protein (0.1 to 1 µm; 10 to 30 per nucleus). PML assembles through its RBCC motif (TRIM family); it is SUMOylated and carries a SUMO-interacting motif, which draws dozens of SUMOylated proteins inside. Roles: sequestering, modifying or degrading these partners; response to oxidative stress and DNA damage, senescence, antiviral defence. Acute promyelocytic leukaemia, t(15;17): the PML::RARA fusion scatters them into micro-speckles; arsenic trioxide, which binds PML, and retinoic acid restore them.
181: A felt of filaments pressed under the inner membrane, between the pores. Cryo-tomography: filaments only 3.5 nm thick (10 nm for cytoplasmic intermediate filaments), about 380 nm long, decorated every 20 nm by their globular domains, all within a 14 nm layer; they cover half of the surface. B-type lamins against the membrane (blue), lamins A and C on the chromatin side (orange): two concentric, overlapping networks. Roles: mechanical strength of the nucleus, anchoring of pores and heterochromatin. At mitosis CDK1 phosphorylates the lamins and the felt dissolves.
183: Two isoforms of the LMNA gene (1q22), by alternative splicing. Prelamin A is farnesylated then cleaved by the protease ZMPSTE24: mature lamin A no longer has a lipid anchor. Abundant in differentiated cells, they set the stiffness of the nucleus. Laminopathies: Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction defects, Dunnigan lipodystrophy, axonal neuropathy. Hutchinson-Gilford progeria: c.1824C>T (p.Gly608=) activates a cryptic splice site in exon 11; progerin, lacking 50 amino acids, loses the cleavage site, stays farnesylated and deforms the envelope.
185: Genes LMNB1 and LMNB2. They keep their farnesyl group, which anchors them in the inner membrane: this is the outermost network. Present in almost all cells from the embryo onwards. LMNB1 duplication: adult-onset autosomal dominant leukodystrophy.
186: In the mouse, during erythroblast maturation, caspase-3 cleaves lamin B and transiently opens the envelope: some of the histones escape, a step required for nuclear condensation before the nucleus is expelled.
187: In the mouse, without lamin B1 or B2, neurons migrate poorly and the cortex is disorganised: the nucleus must withstand deformation during migration.
189: An inner membrane protein with eight transmembrane segments. Its nucleoplasmic domain binds lamin B, HP1 and heterochromatin histones: it is the first system tethering heterochromatin to the envelope, used by young cells; lamins A/C take over during differentiation. Its membrane part is a sterol reductase of the cholesterol pathway. Heterozygous mutation: Pelger-Huët anomaly (hyposegmented neutrophil nuclei); homozygous: Greenberg dysplasia.
191: More than 1,300 domains of 0.1 to 10 Mb touch the lamina, i.e. more than a third of the genome: gene-poor, weakly transcribed, marked by H3K9me2/3, with sharp borders often marked by CTCF. Strings of nucleosomes (11 nm) are drawn here hooked to LBR. Genes that switch on during differentiation often leave the periphery.
193: Emerin, LAP2β, MAN1: inner membrane proteins whose LEM domain binds BAF (small pale bead), a dimer that bridges DNA. They link chromatin to the envelope and the lamina, and help the envelope re-form after mitosis. Emerin (gene EMD, Xq28) is absent in X-linked Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy.
195: A trimer of SUN1 or SUN2 anchored in the inner membrane and held by the lamina; its stalk spans the perinuclear space and its three SUN domains grip the KASH peptides of three nesprins of the outer membrane, themselves linked to actin, microtubules (through kinesin and dynein) and intermediate filaments. LINC transmits cytoskeletal forces to the nucleus: nuclear positioning and migration, mechanotransduction.
197: Two very large, largely disordered proteins rich in serine-arginine repeats. Removing both dissolves speckles. The “SC35” antibody, the historical speckle marker, in fact mostly recognises SRRM2. Loss-of-function variants of SON (ZTTK syndrome) or SRRM2: neurodevelopmental disorders.
199: SRSF1 to SRSF12: one or two RNA-binding domains (RRM) and a tail rich in arginine-serine dipeptides. Phosphorylated by SRPK1 and the CLK kinases, they leave the speckle for genes being transcribed: bound to exons (ESE sequences), they help U1 and U2AF recognise splice sites. Once dephosphorylated, they return.
201: U1, U2, U4/U6 and U5: a small uridine-rich nuclear RNA, a ring of seven Sm proteins (LSm for U6) and specific proteins. Between two rounds of splicing they stay in speckles; they are assembled and retouched in Cajal bodies.
202: A long non-coding RNA of about 8.7 kb, one of the most abundant RNAs in the nucleus, concentrated at the periphery of speckles. Its 3′ end is not polyadenylated: it is cut by RNase P, which releases a small tRNA-like RNA, then protected by a triple helix. It modulates SR protein phosphorylation and alternative splicing; overexpressed in many cancers.
204: Signature protein of the Cajal body (gene COIL). It self-associates through its N-terminus and binds, through its dimethylated arginines, the SMN complex and snRNPs. Without coilin (mouse), Cajal bodies shrink to residual bodies and snRNPs no longer concentrate in them.
205: Small RNAs specific to Cajal bodies, cousins of snoRNAs: box C/D (with fibrillarin) to methylate a ribose at 2′-O, box H/ACA (with dyskerin) to create a pseudouridine — here on snRNAs U1, U2, U4 and U5, at positions that will contact the pre-mRNA. A motif, the CAB box, read by the protein TCAB1 (WRAP53), retains them in the Cajal body. Telomerase RNA carries the same box: without TCAB1, telomerase no longer reaches telomeres.
